items.title: ‘Totally Demonic’: Jonathan Cahn Reveals What Really Happened With the Viral Duct-Taped Man on Plane
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: Whoa.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Celebrated author and Messianic rabbi Jonathan Cahn is making headlines after revealing that he was the unnamed passenger who drew the ire of an allegedly irate man who was so out of control he needed to be duct taped to an airplane seat.

Cahn shared his account of the disturbing incident aboard American Airlines Flight 618, proclaiming that the widely circulated images of a passenger being duct-taped — and media accounts of what unfolded — did not tell the full story.

He told CBN News he was returning home after a number of interviews promoting his new book, “The Altar of Pergamon,” when his assigned seat was unexpectedly changed shortly before the flight. Little did he know that his new placement on the plane would yield an experience he’d never forget.

Cahn ended up sitting beside a man who he said initially appeared friendly. In fact, the two talked for roughly two hours, with the passenger asking about his books and discussing his own family — but then the situation shifted after Cahn prayed about whether God wanted him to share his faith with the man.

“I said, ‘Give me an opening to share salvation with him, and share love with him,’” he said.

According to Cahn, the conversation turned toward faith, and he shared his testimony of once being an atheist and eventually coming to believe in God. Then, he said, the man’s behavior abruptly changed.

“At that moment, I’ve never seen anything like this,” he said. “His face changes. His voice changes.”

Cahn described the transformation as dramatic and spiritual, saying, “It was like someone getting taken over.”

He said the passenger began cursing Jesus and God, making vulgar statements and disturbing other people aboard the aircraft. Cahn said the man later became friendly again before allegedly putting his hands around Cahn’s neck and lightly striking him.

One of the most unusual moments involved Cahn’s laptop. At one point, a black line appeared on his screen. He said the passenger then reached over and tapped the computer, forcing the black area to spread across the entire screen.

Cahn said the computer was particularly important because it contained his writings and other projects.

Then, the author felt God tell him to protect his computer because the devil would use the man to destroy it. Listening to this warning, he attempted to leave his seat with the laptop and alleged that this is when the passenger lunged for it.

“We are wrestling on the plane,” Cahn said, noting that the computer became the focal point of the chaos. “I mean, we are literally wrestling.”

Cahn said the pilot contacted the ground for an emergency landing as the confrontation continued. Eventually, two passengers, including a retired police officer, intervened. Flight attendants provided duct tape to restrain the man, and the plane landed in Baltimore, where authorities took the man into custody.

The irony of the entire incident is that Cohn’s latest book “The Altar of Pergamon” — which came out just before this incident — deals with themes surrounding the devil and spiritual warfare. He believes some of what unfolded on the flight is rooted in that spiritual battle.

“The warfare is real, the enemy is real, and God is real,” he said.

Despite what happened, Cahn said he has no desire to condemn the passenger. Instead, he said he prays for him, and he even delivered a message to him.

“God loves you,” he said. “God’s arms are open. He loves you and He’ll receive you and wash that all away and give you a new beginning.”

Watch the full interview for more on this shocking story.

items.title: Southern Miss Football Coach Makes Bold Faith Declaration Ahead of Big Win
items.author: Tré Goins-Phillips
items.summary: Inspiring.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Football season is just now getting underway, but Southern Miss head coach Blake Anderson drew a lot of attention before his players ever hit the gridiron Saturday.

Ahead of kickoff, Anderson wore a black long-sleeve shirt with the words “Christ Is King” emblazoned in yellow letters across the chest as he and the University of Southern Mississippi team performed took part in the “Eagle Walk” to the stadium.

The team went on to win an impressive 49-3 victory against Alcorn State University.

“I’ve had a bunch of people comment, and I’m pleased that it was noticed,” Anderson said during his weekly press conference. “I mean, the whole point of wearing it was for Christ to be glorified and it to be noticed.”

“I’m super grateful for my bosses that allowed me to be religious [and] use my platform to share my faith,” he continued. “[That is] not probably an easy decision for an AD and a president. But, you know, those are my views. That’s just me trying to use my platform.”

Anderson went on to say he is “saved by grace” and credited God with his success as a coach.

While bold public stances like his often garner criticism, the head football coach said he is thankful the responses online have been overwhelmingly positive.

“You never know what kind of response you’re going to get,” he admitted. “It’s been 99% positive and a few negative, which is what I expected. I wasn’t completely aware of just where it would go.”

He added, “In my opinion, if it makes one person think, then it was worth it.”

Anderson has been vocal about his faith for several years, even through incredible tragedies.

His wife, Wendy, died of breast cancer in 2019, followed soon after by the passing of his father. Anderson’s son, Cason, took his life in 2022, and the coach’s brother, Bryan, died in 2024, following a lengthy battle with aggressive colon cancer.

One of Anderson’s close friends, Larry Fedora, said he “wouldn’t have been able to survive if he didn’t have such a strong faith.”

In 2020, when he was the head coach of Utah State, Anderson told local reporters, “I’m a Christian before I’m anything else. I love the Lord and I feel like God put me in coaching.”

And in an interview five years later with Football Scoop, he said, “My faith comes from Christ, not from me. I’m not tough enough, I’m not big enough to do this on my own.”

items.title: Creed’s Scott Stapp Stopped a Music Festival to Lead Thousands in Worship
items.author: RELEVANT Staff
items.summary: Nobody buys a ticket to a 2000s rock festival expecting a worship service. They went for “Higher” — and then Scott Stapp started talking. Creed closed out the three-day Velocity Festival on Sunday night at the Field of Dreams in Dyersville, Iowa (the actual movie site, cornfield and all)
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

Nobody buys a ticket to a 2000s rock festival expecting a worship service. They went for “Higher” — and then Scott Stapp started talking.

Creed closed out the three-day Velocity Festival on Sunday night at the Field of Dreams in Dyersville, Iowa (the actual movie site, cornfield and all). About 50 minutes into the set, before the band played “What’s This Life For,” Stapp stopped and told the crowd what he’d decided this life was for.

“You know, if you’re trying to figure out what your purpose is in life, what this life is for, I know for me, the more I didn’t surrender to love, the more I didn’t surrender there to God, the more difficulties I had,” he said. “And I remember asking God why. And I felt in my spirit, ‘I got to do what I got to do to get you on your knees, to get you to cry out to me.'”

He kept going.

“So don’t go on living this life without having faith. Faith is taking a risk. It’s believing in something we can’t see, we can’t touch, we can’t feel. I’d rather believe in something than nothing. I’d rather get up here as an imperfect man full of flaws, full of inadequacies, and talk to you about my faith.”

“Because God didn’t come, Christ didn’t come for those who had it all together. He came for the sick. He came for the broken. And that’s all of us.”

Stapp, who is 53 and has spent a good portion of his career being open about the parts of it that went badly, then talked about drinking.

“Think about what kind of story you have. Everything that when I grew up in the church, everything we had to hide,” he said. “That’s part of our testimony now of what God can overcome in our lives. My alcoholism is a victory right now. That’s not something I’m ashamed of. That’s something God got me through.”

“I’m not perfect. I make mistakes. I get up. I pray. I repent. It’s not about rules and regulations. It’s about an authentic life trying to grow and become the best version of you.”

“Don’t ever think you’re not good enough.”

Then he handed it off to the song: “I pray you find what this life is for.”

That was one moment. The other one came about five minutes later. Stapp sang a verse from Brandon Lake’s “Gratitude.” No band behind him. Arms out.

“We’re grateful, my friends,” he said when he finished. “Sing hallelujah.”

Then Creed went into “Weathered.”

People have argued about whether Creed is a Christian band since roughly 1997, and the band has always said no. Sunday didn’t settle it, and Stapp wasn’t trying to. He talked for a few minutes and sang somebody else’s song.

Brandon Lake, coincidentally, is a serious Creed fan — he has worked their songs into his own sets for years. At the end of his 2024 tour, the band turned up and ambushed him with “Higher,” and he sang along without missing a word.

Sunday was the return leg.

items.title: Odors Secular and Sacred: From Game Day to the Lord’s Day
items.author: Daniel Fitzpatrick
items.summary:
Daniel Fitzpatrick

Sports, in the way they have come to inhabit the American imagination, provide us with an image, albeit a corrupted one, of what liturgically oriented living could look like.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Daniel Fitzpatrick

Whatever other superlatives it might also cherish or lament, New Orleans is surely among the most odorous of our cities. This is as much a fact of climate as it is of culture. Slouched between the brackish wavelets of Lake Pontchartrain and the muddy roiling of the Mississippi, the city is saturated in such scents as the sun sucks up from marsh and swamp and bayou. In the heat and humidity, each environ exudes its peculiar miasma, with sea breezes and alluvial funks contending for supremacy. Then, too, as gardenia, crepe myrtle, and magnolia give way to sweet olive and azalea, the city’s cycle of festivity rolls on. Corpus Christi processions incense the avenues. The stoops and portals of our churches exude hints of holy water and chrism. Assumption arrives, and the Blessed Sacrament steams downriver from Baton Rouge as perfumed clouds unfurl from gigantic censers. Passing through the unabating revels of the Vieux Carré, one chances now on the sweet waft of rum, now on a draft of body odor, of weed, of beer, of urine, of étoufée and oysters and fried shrimp, of whatever it is that’s pooled between those bricks. Mardi Gras arrives, and the plastic scent of the beads and the doubloons mingles with the char of fat that drips from roasting flesh. This last spreads richly once again across the city like the aura of a hecatomb when, in the fall, Saints football gets underway.

There looms ever, and especially at the outset of football season, the possibility that all these smells will give way to the flood reek, the rampant stink of mold a hurricane can leave in its wake. 

Whatever the scent in the ascendant now at the end of summer as I write, the NFL season approaches, and millions are dressing the altars of their televisions, garlanding their kitchens in sausages, strewing chips and dips across counters. Something like religious fervor arises, a quality perhaps especially prominent here in New Orleans, where our team, a band of almost perennial disappointments, is called the Saints. Fandom here demands astonishing depths of faith. The outset of the season is a hopeful time too, when at last some respite from summer’s inferno whispers its promise. We love this spectacle, though it end so often in heartbreak. It reminds us, like Melville’s pale usher, dusting his lexicons, of our own mortality and braces us in the face thereof.

Sport does present, after all, a great spectacle not without the capacity to inspire proper wonder. It was not by accident that St. Paul employed his sports metaphors or that many glories of the Old Testament—like Elijah outstripping on foot the chariot of Ahab—comprise feats of athleticism. Great athletes show us the beauty and power of the human body at the limits of its activity. They show us ourselves as we could be—not perhaps as we could be in sports, but as we could be according to the excellence God has in store for us. 

Sports also, in the way they have come to inhabit the American imagination, provide us with an image, albeit a corrupted one, of what liturgically oriented living could look like. Pope John Paul II reminds us in Dies Domini, with reference to Origen, that the true Christian is always living in the Lord’s Day, always enjoying the resurrection. True Lord’s Day engagement has fallen so far in our world that we might wonder if it is even possible anymore. Yet the NFL has successfully trained great swathes of America to live always in Game Day, and the example—if, again, a corrupted one—might offer us means of hope for restoration of greater things.

Consider, for instance, how Game Day has tended to permeate the entirety of the week. Sunday is game day, certainly. But Saturday offers the serene delight of college football, while Friday collects its crowds beneath the lights to watch the high school boys at play. There is Thursday night football, and there is Monday night football. And the sports networks host round-the-clock replays and highlights and analysis so subtle as to boggle the imaginations of the uninitiate. The season goes on. Attention sharpens or subsides according to the way our teams acquit themselves. Heartache. Outrage. Jubilation. And the betting increases and multiplies. And for those who desire it, the joy of game day is available at every moment on the fields and the screens and in the apps. 

This love of the game speaks to the innate desire of the heart to rest in contemplative activity of the highest sort. We want to gaze with friends and family forever on the sum of all beauty and power. We want to belong to something greater than ourselves, something which delights our hearts and gives us back our own being restored and made whole and magnified. And God offers us this in the Lord’s Day, which is not simply a day to be free from work but rather a day to engage in our highest activity—contemplative union with God of the sort we hope to experience in eternity. 

If the mercenary play to which—in the industrial football complex—our culture has devoted itself is the palest shadow of a shadow of the contemplative union of play and prayer offered to us in the Mass, this false American liturgy can nonetheless offer several insights as to how to live always in the Lord’s Day.

The latter, as John Paul II insists, should permeate all of life, and the capacity for that permeation abides already in many places. Mass is not, in most American cities, offered only on Sundays. The sacrifice is available daily. The Liturgy of the Hours and the Rosary, too, train the heart to gather up the experience of time in the light of eternity. And the study of Scripture and the works of the spiritual masters down the centuries offer endless edification to those who seek to learn, in the midst of time, to attend to the God who is always attending to man.

The NFL and its concomitants are instructive, too, with respect to the lavish possibilities of worship. A culture which dedicates billions of dollars annually to a sport makes plain what it values by such sacrifice. Nor do Americans lack examples of the kind of beauty that flourishes when such sacrifice is dedicated instead to worship, to painting and sculpture and mosaic, to incense and gold and all those things that cry this—this! The Lamb’s Supper and Heaven and the salvation of souls—is what we value above all else. From St. Vincent Ferrer in Manhattan to St. Patrick’s Cathedral in New Orleans to the Cathedral Basilica of St. Louis, in a thousand lovely spaces across America, ecclesial beauty abounds, awaiting prayerful attention and recovery and emulation.

Then, too, the joy of the game can recall anew the joy of the Mass. It is easy to live in game day because the delights of game day are obvious. To catch a pass, to score a touchdown, to eat a burger and drink a beer, to see the play of beautiful bodies and rejoice in the capacities of the person—these are joys made simple, the joys of the will at home in itself. The joys of the Lord’s Day arrive often in hiding: joy at the sight of the Eucharist aloft above a simple altar; joy in the presence of family; joy in the prepared meal and the changed diaper and the toddler carried far afield in an evening’s walk. Such joys approach, at times, in secret, in the slow process of recognizing the whisper of the divine will in the people and places and tasks which form the shape of daily life. Such joys come by taking up the cross and allowing for the hard correctives of grace. But the issue is the resurrection, when the scent of the tomb where death lies defeated oozes into nature and makes the sheep to smell at last like the shepherd. 

The medieval poem “The Panther” recalls more than once the odor of holiness, the scent of the Resurrected Lord that flows over the world. That, the poem tells us, was a good stench! Now, with the outset of a new school year, at the end of the summer, the scents of things are specially poignant, bringing with them the ache of what was and the hope for what might be. It is a time for remembering and for being re-membered in the One who draws all to himself, a time for hearing the call to his goodness in the lesser goods, a time to turn from the game of our making to the triune play of God who breathes the odor of salvation.

items.title: Why College Catholics Matter
items.author: Dr. Tod Worner
items.summary:
Dr. Tod Worner

They never stop learning because they never stop wondering. They are wise and not simply smart. The hearts are stirred by vocation. These are the minds that are open to faith.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Dr. Tod Worner

The College Beat: What’s Next

. . .

I recently had a conversation with a friend about Word on Fire’s The College Beat. “With all the issues exploding in the world,” I was asked, “why would a Catholic ministry like Word on Fire dedicate blood, toil, tears, and sweat to cultivating the Catholic faith of college students?” 

My answer is simple. 

It’s because, for Catholicism, this generation is what’s next.

Even though the Gates of Hell will not prevail against the Church, the souls of each generation are molded by the Holy Spirit, the preserved corpus of the Faith, and the living witness of the one or two generations that precede it. And notwithstanding the power of the Holy Spirit and two millennia of preserved intellectual and mystical wisdom, living witnesses are adept either at forming or deforming the faith of the younger generation. That is why data collected a few years ago by Dynamic Catholic, a non-profit organization dedicated to re-energizing the Catholic Church, was particularly disconcerting. It seemed that if you were raised Catholic and you went to college, there was an 85 percent chance that you would stop practicing your faith in college (most in the first year). 

That’s right: 85 percent.

What does that say about the actual impact of our formation? And what does that say about the exquisite malleability of our college students? 

Oof.

If you consider the implications, it means that on a student’s first true foray away from the formative environs of home, parish, and school, they make a seismic and independent decision to walk away from all they have known—their religious and cultural patrimony—without much fanfare, without much regret. Eighteen years of formation (some better than others) gone—and mostly within the first year. Again, how solid is the stuff of our parental formation? And how stern is the stuff of our kids’ faith?

Not very solid. Not very stern. 

Of course, these kids are bright and capable. In his book Excellent Sheep, Yale professor William Deresiewicz marveled at these students’ résumés teeming with evidence of efficiency, multitasking, stress management, and leadership. These kids are smart, and they are going places. As he recalled, 

A friend who teaches at a top university once asked her class to memorize thirty lines of the eighteenth-century poet Alexander Pope. Every single kid got every single line correct, down to the punctuation marks. Seeing them write out the exercise in class, she said, was a thing of wonder, like watching Thoroughbreds circle a track.

But ask them about the deeper things in life, such as their calling, their sense of meaning, or their purpose in life, and they freeze. Somehow along the way, the big things got pushed aside by the small things. Somehow the how of living eclipsed the why. 
Word on Fire’s Liturgy of the Hours is Here!
Order Your Set Today

And the problem is not just a college student’s newfound independence, with its tantalizing morsels of sex, drugs, and ideology on demand. It is also the way many students are taught. Carted through a confusing array of majors and programs, mindsets and mentalities, students often find themselves wandering in a wasteland of materialism, reductionism, and hyperspecialization. In the mad pursuit to do as opposed to be, as eminent Yale Classics professor Donald Kagan lamented, we witness the rise of the functionary and the loss of the “complete man or complete woman.” The complete man or woman is a person gifted with a broader view, a common sense, a hunger for context, and an insatiable curiosity. They never stop learning because they never stop wondering. They are wise and not simply smart. The hearts are stirred by vocation. These are the minds that are open to faith. 

We at Word on Fire are pleased to celebrate the life of the Catholic mind at an incredible array of colleges and universities. From Notre Dame to Princeton, Hillsdale to Yale, Benedictine to Clemson, the University of Texas-Austin to the University of Dallas (among others), our College Beat writers are bright, engaging, inquisitive, and intelligent—and they are Catholic. 

In the wake of a banner year of Catholic conversions worldwide, and especially on college campuses, let’s explore what is on the minds of the Catholic students in the trenches. As they step away from home and onto campus, why do they still step into Mass? These are not an odd, marginalized enclave of believers—they are engaged and involved, passionate and winsome, the best and the brightest. 

So join us every two weeks to read writers who learn or teach on campus. Meet the complete men and women, the discerners and the seekers, the crowd favorites who are also keepers of the faith. 

Let’s renew the faith of the campus. 

Why? 

Because, for Catholicism, this generation is what’s next.
